LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Listen, Understand, Respond & Forgive — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson upgrades the family’s conversations with four words in the right order: ears to the end, the say-back to prove it, the careful answer and the mend that is always ready.

What is this?

Listen runs to the end of the sentence, understand says back what it heard, respond answers with care and forgive keeps the mend on the shelf, ready for whenever the conversation wobbles.

What does it mean?

Most preschool conflicts — and, honestly, most family conflicts — are two people talking and nobody listening. The say-back is the fix: you cannot say back what you did not hear, so the mechanic enforces the virtue.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: listening goes ALL THE WAY to the end (no finishing other people’s sentences); understand is proven, not claimed (the say-back: so you felt left out?); and forgive stays warm on the shelf — the conversation that wobbles can always be mended mid-stream.

Why this matters

This card assembles the class’s final toolset: the earlier peace steps (listen first, think first) and friendship words (forgive) now run as one conversation system — the last skill before the graduation card.

What it teaches

Active listening (the full-ears skill), reflective responding (the say-back), conversational turn-taking, and repair-ready framing — keeping forgiveness within reach during, not only after, the wobble.

Words to learn

listenunderstandrespondforgivesay backall the waymend

Say this to your child

“"Conversations work best in an order. Listen — all the way to the end of what they are saying; not most of the way, not while rehearsing your answer: ALL the way. Understand — prove it with a say-back: so you felt left out when they ran off? A good say-back is worth ten guesses. Respond — now, and only now, your answer: careful, kind, yours. And forgive — keep the word warm the whole time, because conversations wobble sometimes; a misunderstanding, a stepped-on toe, a too-loud voice — the forgiving word is the mend that lets the conversation keep going. Ears, say-back, answer, mend. That is how people who love each other talk."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four conversation words."
  2. Read the panels: the ear-hand girl LISTENs, the nodding boy UNDERSTANDs, the gesturing boy RESPONDs, the peaceful girl FORGIVEs.
  3. Run the listening date below — two minutes, full ears, one say-back each.
  4. Drill the say-back formula on toy drama: bear A complains, bear B must say back ONE thing it heard before answering — "so you felt squashed."
  5. Close with the takeaway: "ears to the end, say it back, answer with care — and keep the forgiving word warm."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the conversation: Listen, a girl listening with a hand to her ear; Understand, a boy nodding with a finger to his chin; Respond, a boy answering with an open gesture; and Forgive, a girl with clasped hands and a peaceful smile — the system drawn as four friendly faces.

Ask your child

"How far does listening go?" "How do we PROVE we understood?" "What stays warm on the shelf?" "What is a say-back?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "So you felt sad when…" (the say-back, deployed on YOU) "I listened all the way!" or the mender: "I forgive you — now where were we?"

Out in the real world

Conversation moments run all day: the sibling’s story that gets interrupted, the instruction half-heard, the hurt feeling half-answered. Install the say-back as the family norm — "before you answer, tell me one thing you heard" — and watch the interruptions starve.

Try it together

The Two-Minute Listening Date: once a day, two minutes, one speaker, one listener. The speaker talks about anything (the dream, the dinosaur, the outrage at lunch). The listener may not interrupt — then must say back ONE thing they heard before commenting. Swap. Grown-ups play too, and get their listening graded (kindly) by the four-year-old. Three dates a week and the say-back starts appearing in wild conversations, unsupervised.

Understanding check

Ask: "How far does listening go? What proves understanding? Where does forgive stay?" To the end, the say-back, warm on the shelf — three answers and the conversation system runs.

Parent tips

Grade the say-back, not the sympathy: "good ears — you caught the dinosaur part" teaches the mechanic; "poor you" teaches nothing repeatable. And model the forgive-mid-stream: "wait — I think I answered too fast and hurt your feelings. I am sorry — say it again, my ears are working now." A child who sees mending happen DURING conversations learns that repair is normal maintenance, not an emergency procedure.

This lesson pairs with the Listen, Understand, Respond & Forgive flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
